intro.html: Three Latin roots run through this topic. cred means believe (you know it from credit and incredible), fid means trust or faith (as in confident), and ver means true (as in very, which first meant “truly”). Spot one of them, and you have a strong clue to the meaning.
cred = believe: credible, incredulous, credulous, credence. fid = trust: fidelity, confidant, diffident. ver = true: veracity, verify, verdict.
Watch the endings: -ible (able to be) makes credible, “able to be believed”; -ulous (inclined to) makes credulous, “inclined to believe,” too easily.

words.ex: Dev’s excuse was hardly {credible}: a dog ate his homework, and he has no dog.
words.ctx: The story seemed far-fetched at first, but it became {credible} once three hikers who had never met described the same strange lights over the lake.
words.etym: From Latin credibilis, from credere, “to believe.”

mn.cue: CRED-ible: can you give it CREDIT?
mn.text: Dev says the dog ate his homework, but Dev has no dog. His teacher gives the story no credit at all: it isn’t {credible}.

scene.alt: A boy claims his dog ate his homework while his teacher, who knows he has no dog, doubts him.

words.def: unwilling or unable to believe something
words.ex: Maya gave an {incredulous} laugh when her little brother said he had cleaned his room.
words.ctx: When the waiter announced that their meal was free, the diners were {incredulous}; they asked him three times whether he was joking.
words.note: A story can be incredible (hard to believe); the person hearing it is incredulous (not believing).

mn.text: Kai says he cleaned his room, but Maya can see socks on the floor and books on the bed. Her raised eyebrows are {incredulous}.

scene.alt: A boy claims his messy room is clean while his sister stares in disbelief.

words.def: too ready to believe things; easily fooled
words.ex: The {credulous} tourist paid ten dollars for a “real” moon rock.
words.ctx: Only the most {credulous} readers believed the website’s claim that a single bean could make a person fly.
words.etym: From Latin credulus, “trusting,” from credere, “to believe.”

mn.text: Rex sells young Lou a “flying potion,” and Lou pays him on the spot without a single question. Lou believes anything: he is {credulous}.

scene.alt: A sneaky seller offers a so-called flying potion to a starry-eyed young man who hands over his coins.

words.def: belief or acceptance that something is true
words.ex: Nobody gave much {credence} to the rumor that school would close for a month.
words.ctx: At first the scientists gave little {credence} to the farmer’s report of a strange new bird, but his clear photographs soon changed their minds.
words.etym: From Latin credentia, from credere, “to believe.”
words.note: We usually give or lend credence: “Her careful notes lent credence to her story.”

mn.cue: CRED-ence: give it CREDIT, believe it
mn.text: Nobody believed Ivy’s story about a fox family in the park, until she showed her photos. The pictures lend {credence} to her story.

scene.alt: A girl holds up her camera to prove her fox story, and her grandfather is convinced.

words.ex: The old dog’s {fidelity} was famous: he waited at the gate every afternoon for his boy.
words.ctx: The translation was praised for its {fidelity}: it kept not only every meaning of the original poem but even its rhythm and rhymes.
words.etym: From Latin fidelitas, from fidelis, “faithful,” from fides, faith.
words.note: High-fidelity (hi-fi) sound is sound that is faithful to the original.

mn.cue: FIDO-lity: loyal as a dog named FIDO
mn.text: Every afternoon at three, Fido waits at the gate for Sami to come home from school, rain or shine. Fido’s {fidelity} never wavers.

scene.alt: A loyal dog waits at the garden gate as his boy runs home from school.

words.def: a trusted friend you can share secrets with
words.ex: Grandpa was Rosa’s {confidant}; she told him things she told no one else.
words.ctx: The young queen trusted few people at court, but her old nurse was her {confidant}, the one person who heard all her worries and never repeated a word.
words.etym: From French confident, from Latin confidere, “to trust fully”: con (thoroughly) + fidere (to trust).
words.note: A confidant (a person you trust; sometimes spelled confidante for a woman) is not confident (sure of yourself).

mn.cue: CONFIDE-ANT: the one you CONFIDE in
mn.text: Rosa confides her biggest worries to Grandpa Gus on the park bench, and he never tells a soul. The person you confide in is your {confidant}.

scene.alt: A teenager whispers a worry to her grandfather on a bench by the river.

words.def: shy and lacking confidence in oneself
words.ex: The {diffident} new student spoke so softly that the teacher asked her to repeat her name.
words.ctx: Though she was the best singer in the choir, Lin was {diffident} about her talent and always asked someone else to take the solo.
words.etym: From Latin diffidere, “to distrust”: dis (not) + fidere (to trust); a diffident person does not trust herself.

mn.text: Lin sings beautifully, but she hides behind the curtain and lets someone else take the solo. She is the opposite of confident: {diffident}.

scene.alt: A shy woman hides her face instead of stepping up to the microphone while a friend urges her on.

words.ex: No one doubted the {veracity} of Nana’s story; she had the photos to prove it.
words.ctx: The reporter checked every quotation with the person who had said it, because the {veracity} of her article mattered more to her than being first.
words.etym: From Latin verax, “truthful,” from verus, true.
words.note: Don’t confuse veracity (truthfulness) with voracity (a huge appetite).

mn.text: Grandpa Gus swears he caught a fish as long as his arm, and this time the photo proves every word. The {veracity} of his story is beyond doubt.

scene.alt: A grandfather holds up a huge fish while a woman snaps a photo to prove his story is true.

words.def: to check or prove that something is true
words.ex: Please {verify} your address before you click send.
words.ctx: The museum would not display the old letter until experts could {verify} that it had been written in 1776, not copied a century later.
words.etym: From Latin verificare, “to make true,” from verus, true.

mn.cue: VER-ify: make sure it’s VERY true
mn.text: Before she buys the old coin, Ada studies it under her magnifying glass, front and back. She wants to {verify} that it is real gold.

scene.alt: A woman examines a gold coin through a magnifying glass to check that it is real.

words.def: a decision or judgment, especially a jury’s
words.ex: After one bite, Grandpa gave his {verdict}: the best chili he had ever tasted.
words.ctx: After two days of listening to witnesses, the jury returned its {verdict}: not guilty on every charge.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin veredictum, “truly said”: vere (truly) + dictum (said).

mn.text: In the case of the missing cake, the jury says what it truly believes: “Not guilty!” The dog wags happily at the {verdict}.

scene.alt: In a courtroom a juror announces “Not guilty!” and the dog on trial wags happily.

head: word
who or what
means
after.cap: Same roots, different jobs: watch whether the word describes the story or the listener.

items.q: Pip told his class that he had ridden a whale to school. His classmates were…
items.why: The listeners did not believe him, so they were incredulous. His story was incredible (hard to believe).

choices: someone who believes an ad promising to make him a millionaire overnight
someone who checks every claim before believing it
someone whose story is easy to believe
items.why: Credulous means too ready to believe. A believable story is credible; a doubter is skeptical or incredulous.

items.q: True or false: a confidant is a person who is very sure of himself.
items.why: False. A confidant is a trusted friend you share secrets with. Sure of yourself is confident.
ver means true (veracity, verify, verdict). cred means believe, fid means trust and dict means say.

items.q: Which sentence uses the right word?
choices: The detective doubted the veracity of the suspect’s alibi.
The hungry bear ate with great veracity.
The veracity of the storm knocked down trees.
items.why: Veracity means truthfulness. A huge appetite is voracity.
